item.content:encoded:
With less than a week until the 2026 MLB playoffs begin, our baseball insiders have been cultivating their sources and are ready to break down the questions, teams and themes that will shape October -- even before the final 12-team postseason field is set.
What is the boldest take we’ve heard from an MLB exec? Is a Los Angeles Dodgers three-peat coming? Can the New York Yankees make a deep run -- with or without Aaron Judge? And who are the sleeper teams and under-the-radar players to watch?
Here’s the latest intel our MLB experts are hearing as Jeff Passan, Buster Olney, Jesse Rogers, Jorge Castillo and Alden Gonzalez empty their notebooks heading into the playoffs.
What is the boldest prediction you’ve heard from an MLB exec or scout?
Olney: The Padres are going to win the World Series for the first time in their history, with just about everything trending in the right direction. “Once you get into the postseason with all of the built-in off days, that’s going to help their bullpen -- which is the best,” he noted. The Padres’ starting pitching is the team’s biggest concern, but as the Dodgers demonstrated in 2024, you can win with three or four functional starters who are backed by a deep bullpen.
Passan: The Red Sox might be the No. 5 seed, but they’re going to win the American League pennant. Since the All-Star break, one evaluator pointed out, the Red Sox have the best offense in the AL. They’re also an MLB best in Fielding Independent Pitching, a predictive metric that suggests they will continue to throw well. It’s a deep bullpen. It’s a solid-enough rotation. It’s a productive lineup. And, perhaps most helpful of all, it’s the AL, where the path to the World Series is a sandy beach compared to the jungle of the National League.
Do MLB insiders think the Dodgers will turn it on in October again like they did the past two postseasons?
Gonzalez: The general sentiment about the Dodgers seems to be this: They’ll be the favorites until proven otherwise. That’s what they’ve elevated to. They’re too talented, too deep, and they’ve become too adept at navigating seasons to have many detractors, regardless of whatever adversity they might face.
These past couple of weeks have offered a perfect snapshot. The Dodgers’ offense was a serious concern, but now -- with Mookie Betts, Teoscar Hernandez and Kyle Tucker on a heater, and Shohei Ohtani back -- not so much. Their bullpen was, too, but Edwin Diaz has looked sharp since coming back, Roki Sasaki could once again become a weapon and Emmet Sheehan might be too. Regardless, their rotation is widely expected to be an equalizer.
Passan: They’re still the favorites, which is saying something when considering the fatigue that often attaches itself to dynastic teams. But the Dodgers have shown enough vulnerabilities that a number of evaluators believe another team will represent the NL in the World Series. One GM’s sentiment -- “I’d take every NL playoff team over every AL playoff team,” he said -- speaks to the sort of competition the Dodgers will face.
And with so many question marks about how Ohtani and Andy Pages and Blake Snell will fare after returning on the eve of the postseason with no rehab assignments, the Dodgers are not nearly the sure thing they’ve been in recent postseasons. At the same time, they remain, top to bottom, the most talented team in the game, and nobody would be surprised if they win their third consecutive World Series.
How much faith does the industry have in the Rays and Brewers turning the best regular-season records into World Series appearances?
Olney: There is more faith in the Brewers than I’ve ever heard, because the general perception is that they are just a better, deeper team than the group that was bulldozed by the Dodgers in last year’s postseason -- and they’ve got the best starting pitcher, in Jacob Misiorowski. “I think he might hit 107 [mph] in the playoffs,” speculated one evaluator, assessing the impact of the adrenaline, expectations and Misiorowski’s heightened competitiveness. And generally, there is a lot of respect for the Rays, particularly when measured against the low bar of the American League.
Rogers: As much as ever. The Brewers have more believers this year than last simply based on the top of their rotation led by Misiorowski and Logan Henderson. Their depth there is better as well. Robert Gasser has come on strong while rubber-armed Aaron Ashby is a key bullpen guy to go along with Abner Uribe and Trevor Megill.
On the Rays side, their draw for the postseason isn’t perfect -- according to one insider -- but if the Yankees and Red Sox play three games in the wild-card round, it’ll set things up nicely for them in the division series. After that, they’ll be heavy favorites to get to the Fall Classic.
Given Aaron Judge’s health questions, do those in the game think the Yankees will make another deep October run?
Castillo: Opinions vary around the majors. One front office executive said the Yankees have “no chance” of making a World Series run without Judge. Another said he believes it’s possible behind the pitching staff, though the executive added that the bullpen is seemingly running on fumes down the stretch.
Anything can happen in a three-game series. The Red Sox nearly bounced New York last year, falling short in Game 3 thanks to Cam Schlittler’s sterling performance.
After that, the Rays are reminiscent of the Blue Jays club that gave the Yankees trouble last year -- from the regular season through eliminating them in four games in the ALDS. Not having Judge undoubtedly hurts the Yankees’ chances of surviving the gauntlet.
Olney: It wouldn’t be a surprise if they emerge in the American League -- and nor would it be a surprise if they got knocked out in the first round. Without Judge, they are vulnerable against left-handed pitching, and Boston is loaded with lefties.
If they do survive the Red Sox, then they’ll open the division series on the road in the Trop, where they don’t match up well; the Rays’ style of play on their home surface caused all kinds of problems for the Yankees this year.
That all said, the Yankees have the best pitching of the AL teams; they have a good lineup (albeit not great); and their defense has improved.
Who else do MLB insiders feel could be this October’s most dangerous teams?
Rogers: As easy as it would be to pick an AL team to make a surprising run simply because the draw there is softer, experts like the Padres as a dangerous lower-seeded team. They have a good playoff formula now that the rotation has some help and the lineup is hitting for power. In fact, San Diego leads MLB in home runs in September. And of course, they have that vaunted bullpen.
With Aaron Judge on the shelf, the Red Sox are becoming a favorite pick among experts in the AL. Others point to Yankees pitching as their key to advancing. It’s really good behind Cy Young fave Cam Schlittler.
Gonzalez: The Phillies are often a popular pick for this question, and this year it’s no different. They have obvious flaws, from the makeup of their bullpen to their overall defense to, mostly, the status of Jesus Luzardo. But they have a bevy of top-shelf stars, the type that tend to make a major impact on October. They have the experience of having navigated these stakes as a group many times. They have a raucous home environment, one that arguably trumps any in the sport. And, lately, they have Aaron Nola looking like his vintage self.
Still: it’s hard to dismiss the Luzardo factor in all this. He changes everything. “If he’s healthy,” a rival front office executive said, “they’re my answer.” If not, he added, the Brewers are the better, more well-rounded team. Luzardo is that important.
Who are some under-the-radar players with industry buzz as potential postseason stars?
Castillo: Rays outfielder Victor Mesa Jr., Brewers first baseman Jake Bauers and Padres first baseman Ty France. Mesa, dumped in a trade by the Marlins in February, surfaced from Triple-A in late May to join Junior Caminero, Yandy Diaz and Jonathan Aranda as dangerous bats. Bauers and France are veterans who lead their respective teams in wRC+ this season -- indicating, at least by that measure, that they’ve been the best hitters on their clubs -- and have been overshadowed.
Passan: In an era when the average fastball is 94.6 mph and pitchers throw it around 30% of the time, Cleveland left-hander Parker Messick and Milwaukee right-hander Logan Henderson are anomalies.
Messick, 25, is a favorite of scouts. He throws a four-seamer that averages 94 mph more than 40% of the time, and despite the relative lack of velocity, it’s been a banger of a pitch, the third-most-valuable heater in MLB behind Jacob Misiorowski’s and Cam Schlittler’s.
Henderson leans even more heavily on his fastball (45.7%) even though it’s slower (93.1 mph) and it has the sixth-highest run value.
Why do they work so well? Messick and Henderson both have exceptional control, and as much as velo rules the modern game, there is still room for pitching artistry, and they personify it.

item.content:encoded:
We’re down to the final days of the 2026 regular season with still quite a number of teams that have something to play for -- including a few who are fighting for their postseason lives.
Such is the case with the Astros and Rangers, who are tied atop the AL West (with Houston owning the tiebreaker); the team that loses the division will most likely miss the playoffs entirely. Elsewhere in the American League, the Guardians and White Sox are still battling for the division title, though the loser of that should slot into the third wild-card spot.
While all the divisions in the National League have been clinched already, the wild-card race, specifically in terms of seeding, is very much heating up, with the Phillies, Cubs and Padres entering play on Wednesday in a three-way tie.
Which clubs will get to keep playing into October? And which will watch their playoff aspirations come to an end?
Our expert panel has ranked every team based on a combination of what we’ve seen so far and what we already knew going into the 162-game marathon that is a full baseball season. We also asked ESPN MLB experts Bradford Doolittle, Buster Olney and Jorge Castillo to weigh in with an observation for all 30 teams.
1. Milwaukee Brewers
Record: 99-59
Previous ranking: 1
With the season down to a handful of games, the Brewers have all but run out of time for Kyle Harrison to recover his first-half form. Harrison was 8-2 with a 3.01 ERA before the break; he’s 2-3 with a 7.80 ERA since. His strikeout rate has remained steady, even as his velocity and movement measures have become more volatile. Meanwhile, his walk rate has more than doubled, and his homers-allowed rate has nearly tripled. Suffice to say, this is not a great combination of trends. Milwaukee has tried to get Harrison back in stride by using him out of the bullpen, but he’s gotten hammered as a reliever. Brewers fans who dreamed of a big three rotation of Jacob Misiorowski, Harrison and Logan Henderson probably need to recalibrate their expectations at this point. -- Doolittle
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Record: 97-61
Previous ranking: 2
We’re nearing October baseball, and it’s as if the Dodgers are knocking off items on a to-do list. Shohei Ohtani back in the lineup? Check. Edwin Diaz finding his stuff, finally? Check. Will Smith back in the lineup? Check -- and he has an OPS of close to 1.000 this month. Mookie Betts back to being Mookie Betts? Check. Kyle Tucker digging out of his seasonlong slump? Check. L.A. is putting the pieces back together just in time as it begins its effort to become the first NL team to go back-to-back-to-back. -- Olney
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Record: 96-62
Previous ranking: 3
Tampa Bay began the season with the longest odds to win the AL East. On Tuesday, it clinched its first division title since 2021 with a win over the Yankees. The Rays will enter their first postseason since 2023 as the favorites to win the AL pennant behind a distinct home-field advantage at Tropicana Field, a strong pitching staff and a dynamic lineup centered around MVP candidate Junior Caminero, designated hitter Yandy Diaz and first baseman Jonathan Aranda. With a payroll that ranks 28th in the majors, the Rays seek to become the team with the lowest-ranked payroll to ever win the World Series. -- Castillo
4. Atlanta Braves
Record: 93-65
Previous ranking: 5
Atlanta would’ve preferred to get a first-round bye in the playoffs, of course, but the fact that the Brewers and Dodgers seemed to have locked down the No. 1 and No. 2 seeds allows the Braves to treat this last week of the regular season like the last week of spring training. They can plot out the best way to rest their key relievers, assess the progress of Robert Suarez and arrange at-bats for the position players to be primed for the postseason. Meanwhile, the teams the Braves are likely to face in the first round -- the Phillies, Cubs and Padres -- are all still pushing for berths and home-field advantage in the wild-card round. -- Olney
5. New York Yankees
Record: 91-67
Previous ranking: 4
Despite manager Aaron Boone saying on Tuesday that Aaron Judge isn’t expected to return from his calf strain in time for the wild-card round, Judge told ESPN the following day that he does in fact intend to be ready for Game 1. He suffered the injury last Wednesday and was placed on the injured list two days later. The Yankees were initially cryptic about the setback, declining to disclose the severity and Judge’s outlook.
Boone offered some clarity Tuesday when he called it a “moderate strain” and acknowledged that the club does not plan on having him to open the postseason. Judge received a PPP injection Monday. The Yankees hope that will spur recovery. Otherwise, New York faces an uphill challenge to survive in October without its three-time MVP at his best. -- Castillo
6. Chicago Cubs
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 6
No player has made more of a second-half leap than Alex Bregman, whose season has just gathered momentum almost daily since the last week of July. That momentum was stopped in its tracks when Bregman suffered facial fractures last weekend when struck by a foul ball. The good news is that the Cubs decided against placing Bregman on the IL, believing he might be ready for the playoffs after.
But even if that proves to be optimistic, Cubs fans can take solace in the presence of icy-cool rookie Pedro Ramirez. The Cubs didn’t drop off much when Dansby Swanson was injured, as Ramirez provided a league-average bat and glove work at both second and third base that has kept an elite Cubs defense on track. You want Bregman in there, for sure -- but Ramirez provides a heck of a Plan B. -- Doolittle
7. San Diego Padres
Record: 88-70
Previous ranking: 8
San Diego’s magic number for clinching a playoff spot is shrinking, allowing general manager A.J. Preller and skipper Craig Stammen the chance to line up their staff for the wild-card series, with options developing. Stammen indicated to reporters that unless Michael King is needed to clinch a playoff spot on the last day of the regular season, he will be held over to start Game 1 of the wild card, wherever that is -- so he wouldn’t necessarily be used Sunday in order to win home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs.
Additionally, the Padres are in a better position to rest their bullpen, the perceived strength of the team. Adrian Morejon ranks third among all relievers in innings. Rest might be overrated for Mason Miller: He has made 16 appearances on zero days’ rest, and in those games, he has allowed two hits and one earned run in 16⅔ innings, with two walks and 27 strikeouts. -- Olney
8. Philadelphia Phillies
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 7
The culture of Philadelphia’s starting pitchers, from Zack Wheeler to Cristopher Sanchez to Aaron Nola, is to pitch deep into games. Unlike so many starters in this generation, Wheeler takes the mound expecting to work into the late innings -- and the Phillies will need this sort of production from the rotation, given the team’s recent bullpen problems. Orion Kerkering, an important part of the relief corps, struggled so badly that he was sent to the minors last week. Jose Alvarado has pitched better down the stretch, and hard-throwing Alex MacFarlane has quickly ascended into an important role in his rookie season in the bullpen. But the Phillies’ rotation will carry the team’s October dreams. -- Olney
9. Boston Red Sox
Record: 85-73
Previous ranking: 9
The Red Sox rewarded Chad Tracy on Tuesday for leading the team’s historic turnaround by removing his interim tag and giving him a three-year contract to continue as manager. Now he’ll look to accomplish what his predecessor Alex Cora couldn’t last year: beating the Yankees on the road in the AL Wild Card Series.
Boston has cooled off since going 32-5 to put itself in playoff position and faces some injury uncertainty going into October. Ceddanne Rafaela returned Tuesday after missing 16 games with a quad injury, and Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch on his right hand last Thursday and is dealing with soreness. On the mound, the Red Sox could receive two significant reinforcements for the bullpen in Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck. Crochet, last season’s AL Cy Young runner-up, has been out with a shoulder injury since late April, while Houck hasn’t appeared in a game in 2026. -- Castillo
10. Cleveland Guardians
Record: 82-76
Previous ranking: 12
Cleveland is, once again, showing its knack for a strong finishing kick. Over the past decade, only the Dodgers have won more September games. For Guardians fans aching for their team’s first title since the Truman administration, October is a higher priority at this point.
Like the White Sox, the first order of business is to secure the AL Central title and the first-round bye likely to go with it. Given the neck-and-neck nature of Cleveland’s battle with Chicago, there likely isn’t going to be much time for manager Stephen Vogt to ease up on the pedal to finish the season. That would be nice to do when it comes to rookie ace Parker Messick, who will finish the season with at least 50 more innings than he has ever thrown in a season. Messick has shown no signs of fatigue, so it may not matter. -- Doolittle
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
Record: 84-74
Previous ranking: 10
Manager Torey Lovullo’s comments in a radio interview last week in which he acknowledged that the Diamondbacks “probably” -- his word -- need to reach the postseason to earn him a contract extension surprised many in the industry, as Lovullo has a strong and long-standing relationship with his boss, Mike Hazen. The Ketel Marte situation has been challenging for the organization, with the team’s highest-paid position player failing to show up to the park, and owner Ken Kendrick has a reputation for being mercurial and demanding. Lovullo’s contract runs out at season’s end, and he and the Diamondbacks agreed they would discuss his status then. -- Olney
12. Chicago White Sox
Record: 81-77
Previous ranking: 11
The White Sox have wobbled down the stretch, but they have not fallen down. It looks like they will join the playoff party, completing an incredible two-year turnaround that saw them go from setting the modern single-season loss record to playing in October.
Barring a face-plant over the last few days of the season, the question of whether the Sox can overtake Cleveland for the AL Central title is the biggest remaining question. It’s impactful, with a first-round bye likely on the line. A bye is a boon for any team, but among likely postseason entrants, it might loom largest for the White Sox. That’s just because of how manager Will Venable has had to stretch his pitching resources to the maximum just to get to this point. A wild-card skip would give his staff at least a little time to regroup before the ALDS begins. -- Doolittle
13. Pittsburgh Pirates
Record: 80-78
Previous ranking: 14
Why did Paul Skenes lapse into baseball’s pitching middle class rather than continue his march toward Cooperstown? There is no bigger task for the Pirates and Skenes this offseason than figuring this out. With one more start to go, he has already allowed more runs this season than he did in his first two seasons combined. To be sure, it’s not all on Skenes, whose expected ERA, 3.27 per Statcast, is unusually divergent from his actual ERA (3.91). Still, even a 3.27 ERA is a far cry from the level of effectiveness Skenes flashed before this season. Why? Finding the answer to that question could prove to be the biggest addition Pittsburgh makes this winter. -- Doolittle
14. Texas Rangers
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 16
With eyes on the disappointing Mariners and Yordan Alvarez’s Triple Crown watch, the Rangers quietly remained in contention in the historically dreadful AL West all summer. Following three straight losses, they now find themselves tied atop the division with Houston. Texas will host the Mets in a series finale Thursday before finishing the season with three games in Minnesota. The Rangers will need to finish with a better record than the Astros, who own the tiebreaker, to reach the postseason for the first time since winning the 2023 World Series. -- Castillo
15. Houston Astros
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 13
The Astros fired general manager Dana Brown last month and are under .500 with four games remaining ... but they still have a real chance to win the division. That’s the AL West in 2026. The Astros finish the regular season with a four-game series in West Sacramento against an A’s team that has an MLB-worst run differential. The bad news: The Astros head there tied atop the division. The good news: They hold the tiebreaker over Texas. In the background over the last few days of the season: Alvarez’s push to become the first player to win a Triple Crown since Miguel Cabrera in 2013. -- Castillo
16. Toronto Blue Jays
Record: 77-82
Previous ranking: 15
The Blue Jays did not replicate their 2025 magic in 2026, largely due to injuries and their offense falling off a cliff. They finished last season fourth in the majors with a 112 wRC+; this season, they’re tied for 24th with a 95 wRC+. The dropoff starts with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and George Springer. Guerrero has nine home runs -- and, inexplicably, just one at home -- with a .695 OPS in the first year of a 14-year, $500 million contract extension. Springer, who reversed a precipitous decline to hit 32 home runs with a .959 OPS last season, has 15 home runs with a .730 OPS in 124 games this year -- and he’s a free agent after this season. Whether Springer re-signs or not, a rebound in 2027 starts with Guerrero sparking an offense that is tied for last in home runs in 2026. -- Castillo
17. Miami Marlins
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 18
Here’s the good news about the Marlins’ 2026 season: They hung around all year, battling among the contenders and having some individual successes. Here’s what’s not-so-great about where they stand right now: It’s hard to identify the players who could lead a Miami breakout into full-scale contention with the best NL teams.
Otto Lopez had an excellent season, but he’ll turn 28 years old next week and his OPS is under .800. Griffin Conine is the one player on the team with an OPS over .800, and he’s 29. Sandy Alcantara reestablished himself as a rotation leader, but he’s 31. Eury Perez has flashes of dominance and is just 23, but he’s got an injury history and will finish this season with an ERA over 4.00. More depth and more talent is needed for the Marlins to take the next step. -- Olney
18. Baltimore Orioles
Record: 78-81
Previous ranking: 19
Another disappointing season in Baltimore has already prompted some changes in the front office, but not at the top. President of baseball operations Mike Elias is expected to return in 2027. One move his front office got right was signing Pete Alonso last winter. The first baseman, who has played in every game this season, hit his 40th home run of the season in Monday’s win over the Blue Jays. He clearly isn’t why the Orioles aren’t going to the postseason for the second straight year.
Baltimore’s young position player core has not lived up to the hype, while the pitching staff wasn’t good enough to shoulder the load. Elias & Co. already decided to move on from former No. 1 pick Adley Rutschman, an All-Star catcher previously considered a foundational player, at the trade deadline. More significant moves could come this offseason. -- Castillo
19. St. Louis Cardinals
Record: 77-81
Previous ranking: 17
This rebuilding season has been an unqualified success for the Cardinals. If not for a leaky bullpen, their soft wild-card contention might have been a lot more solid. While bullpens are sometimes the final piece of the contention puzzle for a building team, that’s not always the case. Some clubs develop a bullpen-building process that takes effect even as the rest of the roster remains a work in progress. The Pirates of recent vintage are a good example.
Thus, the project of putting together a contention-worthy bullpen is a crucial one for the Chaim Bloom-led front office. Bloom was part of a Rays front office that annually churned out elite, no-name bullpens. However, during the four years that Bloom led the Red Sox front office, Boston ranked 24th in bullpen ERA (4.48) and middle-of-the-pack in save percentage. Good first year, but there is more to prove in St. Louis. -- Doolittle
20. Detroit Tigers
Record: 74-85
Previous ranking: 20
The Tigers will probably finish fourth in the AL in run differential, perhaps third if they pass the Red Sox, and will easily pace the Central by that measure. When you consider that, along with Detroit’s freakishly bad record in one- and two-run games (now 21-51) and the relatively short list of players on expiring deals (Jack Flaherty and Gleyber Torres, along with the retiring Justin Verlander), the Tigers are an obvious and very strong bounce-back candidate for the 2027 season. That doesn’t mean that president of baseball operations Scott Harris and his staff don’t have their work cut out for them when it comes to evaluating this lackluster season. Still, for the Tigers’ disappointed fans, it’s important to keep in mind that their team will be proceeding from a relative position of strength. -- Doolittle
21. Washington Nationals
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 23
In so many ways, the 2026 season was a success for the Nationals, who exceeded expectations this year, flirting with contention in the first half and seeing the development of players like CJ Abrams and James Wood into offensive stars. But the team’s pitching collapsed in the second half -- Washington’s second-half ERA of 4.49 ranks 25th. The Nationals locked down Cade Cavalli to a multiyear deal last week at the end of what has been a breakout season, but it’s clear that president of baseball operations Paul Toboni’s greatest challenge is to develop the sort of pipeline of pitching that will allow them to compete with the big-market teams in the division. -- Olney
22. Seattle Mariners
Record: 74-84
Previous ranking: 24
A year after falling one win short of the franchise’s first World Series appearance, the Mariners’ season will end Sunday with a whimper. The 2026 campaign will be remembered as the most disappointing one in franchise history.
Cal Raleigh’s drop-off from 60 home runs and an MVP runner-up finish was baffling. Julio Rodriguez regressed and still hasn’t made the superstar jump widely expected of him. Josh Naylor was a below-average hitter in the first year of his five-year contract. The starting rotation was not as good as advertised. Changes are inevitable, likely starting with manager Dan Wilson. But the Mariners can’t fire all of their players. They’ll need their core to bounce back from down seasons in order to rebound in 2027. -- Castillo
23. New York Mets
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 21
No one will go into the 2027 season under more pressure than David Stearns, the Mets’ head of baseball operations, following their collapse down the stretch in 2025 and the poor 2026 season. So it makes sense that he worked to keep someone he has a working relationship with in the managerial role, Andy Green, who had his interim tag removed and was hired to a three-year deal Tuesday. Steve Cohen’s comments on an SNY broadcast about needing new voices within the organization got the attention of a lot of rival executives, who wondered if the impact of Pete Alonso’s encore performance at Citi Field and the “Fire Stearns” chants last week made an impression on the owner. Under the circumstances, hiring Green seems like the right move for Stearns, the smart move. -- Olney
24. Minnesota Twins
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 22
The arrival of prospects Kaelen Culpepper, Walker Jenkins and Emmanuel Rodriguez has the Twins’ prospective 2027 position group in good shape even if veteran Josh Bell declines his mutual option and departs. The murkiest position is catcher, where Ryan Jeffers is likely headed for free agency, presumably after the Twins issue him a qualifying offer. The QO could limit Jeffers’ market, but probably not that much, as Jeffers looks like the best free agent catcher option out there. If he leaves, the Twins will need someone to pair with Caratini.
Long term, after drafting Vahn Lackey third in the most recent draft, the Twins seem in good shape with him, Eduardo Tait, Khadim Diaw and Carson Tinney all showing well in prospect rankings. Alas, none of that quartet is likely to be a 2027 solution. -- Doolittle
25. Cincinnati Reds
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 25
The ongoing maturation of Elly De La Cruz, as he edges toward his career prime, has provided ample reason to keep an eye on the Reds, even amid a last-place showing. Still, there have been enough trade rumors regarding the supremely talented shortstop to make you wonder just how long De La Cruz will be around.
Recent comments made by his agent, Scott Boras, don’t help. Boras suggested to reporters that a future foray into the open market made more sense for De La Cruz than a below-market extension. What does that mean for the Reds in the near term? For now, he has three more years of team control, so there’s no reason to be rash. Still, with this cloud starting to form over Great American Park, some sort of clarity about how the Reds plan to deal with their best player would be nice. -- Doolittle
26. Kansas City Royals
Record: 68-90
Previous ranking: 26
The Royals’ biggest offseason project will be to figure out their 2027 bullpen formula. That process begins with evaluating the relievers already on hand. Presumed closer Carlos Estevez had shoulder surgery -- bafflingly not until the second week of September -- and the Royals almost certainly won’t pick up their 2027 club option on him. Lucas Erceg looked lost before being shipped off to Omaha, but he performed well in Triple-A and his velocity upon his return to the majors has been at its highest level all year. Which Erceg is the real one? Is journeyman righty Nate Pearson a leverage option? Does Craig Kimbrel have anything left? The Royals will need relief help from outside the organization, but how much of it will depend on the outcome of these evaluations and others. -- Doolittle
27. San Francisco Giants
Record: 65-94
Previous ranking: 27
The general perception of San Francisco’s farm system is that it improved in 2026, and Bryce Eldridge established himself as a player the organization could build around. Beyond that, however, the Giants really haven’t progressed. They have a top-heavy payroll situation, with hundreds of millions owed to Rafael Devers, Willy Adames and Matt Chapman. The questions about manager Tony Vitello making the jump from college to professional baseball weren’t quelled by his first season with the Giants -- and neither were the questions about the man who hired him, Buster Posey, who is still relatively new to his front office role. -- Olney
28. Athletics
Record: 63-95
Previous ranking: 28
The A’s are stumbling to the finish line having lost 95 games. All-Star catcher Shea Langeliers recently returned from knee surgery, but several other prominent players remain on the IL, including Nick Kurtz, Tyler Soderstrom, Jacob Wilson, Brent Rooker, Luis Severino and Gage Jump. They’ll enter their season-ending series against the Astros with a negative-217 run differential -- the worst in the majors by 33 runs. With one season remaining before the A’s move to Las Vegas in 2028, they enter the winter in search of a general manager after David Forst’s departure in early August. Their offseason priorities are straightforward: Get healthy and improve a pitching staff that has a 5.43 ERA (29th) despite pitching half its games at the launchpad known as Sutter Health Park. -- Castillo
29. Los Angeles Angels
Record: 60-98
Previous ranking: 29
The Angels, despite 11 straight losing seasons, are the only franchise in the majors that has yet to post a 100-loss season. That could change this weekend in Seattle, where the Angels will need to win three of four games to avoid reaching the century mark. It’d be a fitting conclusion to Arte Moreno’s tenure as owner. Last month, Moreno agreed to sell controlling interest in the team to Stan Kroenke for a record valuation of $4 billion. Kroenke will take over a franchise that has not appeared in the postseason since 2014 and has not won a postseason game since 2009.
The first order of business this offseason will be hiring fired general manager Perry Minasian’s replacement. The team could also be in search of a manager to replace Kurt Suzuki, who is on a one-year contract. It is a transformative time in Anaheim. -- Castillo
30. Colorado Rockies
Record: 57-101

Colorado has compiled 100 losses for the fourth consecutive season; the last team to suffer 100-plus losses in five consecutive seasons were the Phillies, from 1938 to 1942. In Paul DePodesta’s first year of running Colorado’s baseball operations, there were some under-the-hood improvements: the biggest run differential improvement of all 30 teams in 2026, an improved farm system and some nice finds for the every-day lineup, like Jake McCarthy, TJ Rumfield and Connor Norby. There’s still a long way to go to competitive relevance for the Rockies, especially given the high bar required in the Dodgers’ NL West. -- Olney

Los Tampa Bay Rays, equipo del mexicano Jonathan Aranda, aseguraron el liderato de la División Este de la Liga Americana tras vencer 6-1 a los New York Yankees en el segundo juego de la doble cartelera disputada este martes por la noche en el Bronx.
El conjunto de Florida conquista el título divisional por primera vez desde 2021 y buscará trasladar el nivel mostrado durante la temporada regular a los playoffs.

Jonathan Aranda mantiene una temporada de alto nivel con los Rays
Jonathan Aranda sostiene una temporada destacada con los Tampa Bay Rays y se consolida como uno de los bateadores de contacto más constantes tanto del equipo como de las Grandes Ligas.
El mexicano ocupa el sexto lugar de la Liga Americana en imparables, con 157. También suma 22 cuadrangulares y 92 carreras impulsadas, cifra que lo coloca entre los seis mejores productores de carreras del circuito.
Su camino hacia MLB comenzó hace poco más de una década, cuando fue firmado desde la Academia de Toros de Tijuana. A partir de entonces recorrió el sistema de sucursales hasta llegar al primer equipo de Tampa Bay en 2022.
PUBLICIDAD
La gran temporada de los Rays y su camino en los playoffs
Los Tampa Bay Rays han tenido una temporada regular consistente que les aseguró un lugar en la postemporada. El equipo mantiene una marca de 96-61, la mejor de la Liga Americana, con cinco juegos todavía por disputar.
Con ese desempeño, Tampa Bay aseguró el descanso durante la ronda de comodines y avanzó de manera directa a la siguiente fase. Ahora espera conocer a su rival en la Serie Divisional.
De mantenerse las posiciones en la recta final del calendario, los New York Yankees y los Boston Red Sox se enfrentarían en la ronda de comodines por el pase ante los Rays. El panorama aún podría modificarse en los últimos juegos de la campaña regular.
PUBLICIDAD
Si Boston atraviesa una mala racha, Chicago White Sox podría alcanzarlo en la clasificación, pues se encuentra a tres juegos de los Red Sox con cinco juegos por delante.
En ese escenario, los White Sox también surgirían como posibles rivales de Tampa Bay en la postemporada.
Cómo marcha el panorama de cara a la postemporada en las demás divisiones
Los New York Yankees y los Boston Red Sox ya aseguraron su lugar en la postemporada como equipos comodín. Aun así, Boston podría pasar del segundo al tercer puesto de la clasificación, dependiendo de los resultados en la recta final de la temporada.
Los Chicago White Sox mantienen, por ahora, el último boleto disponible a los playoffs. Sin embargo, todavía tienen presión de otros equipos que buscan alcanzarlos: los Texas Rangers se encuentran a tres juegos, mientras que los Toronto Blue Jays y los Baltimore Orioles permanecen más rezagados, a cinco victorias de distancia.

Sin embargo, el equipo de la Ciudad de los Vientos todavía aspira a ser campeón de la División Central de la Liga Americana, los Cleveland Guardians conservan una ventaja de apenas un juego, por lo que todavía no tienen asegurado el primer lugar.
La lucha por el título de la División Oeste de la Liga Americana también se mantiene abierta. Los Houston Astros y los Texas Rangers tienen el mismo récord, por lo que el campeón divisional se definirá en los últimos juegos del calendario regular.
Pasando a la Liga Nacional, la disputa se concentra en los puestos de comodín, ya que las divisiones tendrían definidos a sus líderes. Los Atlanta Braves encabezan el Este y los Milwaukee Brewers dominan la Central, mientras que los Dodgers nuevamente se adueñaron del Oeste.

NEW YORK -- Back in Spring Training, the preseason predictions and projection systems were skeptical of the Rays. After consecutive fourth-place finishes, they were widely picked to finish last in the American League East this year.
Those doubts persisted throughout an up-and-down start to the season. They seemed to reappear every time the Rays stumbled through a brief losing streak. Slights surfaced in other ways, too, with pundits repeatedly referring to other clubs as the team to beat in a division led by Tampa Bay.
Now, there can be no doubt. The Rays are once again AL East champions, and the road to the World Series in the AL will run through Tropicana Field.
“I don't think anything was handed to us all year. Obviously, I think a lot of guys expected [the Yankees] to run away with it, and [it] probably to be New York, Boston and Toronto at the top,” veteran starter Nick Martinez said. “No one really expected us to be here, so we've had to fight for it from the beginning of the season.”
Fittingly, the Rays had to fight to make it official on Tuesday night. After a 2-0 loss in Game 1 of a doubleheader at Yankee Stadium, the Rays held on to win Game 2, 6-1, behind a dominant performance by ace Drew Rasmussen, who struck out 11 on a career-high 114 pitches and carried a no-hit bid into the seventh inning.
In what was expected to be a four-team race, the fifth team finished first.
“Four teams got all the attention in this division, and they're four really good teams, right?” president of baseball operations Erik Neander said. “Just a testament to these guys and just an unbelievable year, and they deserve this. They deserve to enjoy this.”
That they did.
After shortstop Taylor Walls scooped a grounder from George Lombard Jr. and fired it to first baseman Jonathan Aranda for the final out, the team poured onto the field for handshakes, high fives and hugs. Coaches, players and staff changed into AL East “CHAMPS” shirts and hats and gathered in front of the mound for a team photo, then took the celebration inside.
The Rays popped bottles of champagne, poured beer, sprayed silly string, smoked cigars and danced. Manager Kevin Cash started the party with a reminder that they want to do this three more times next month.
“This group has deserved it all year long, and it's a special group,” Yandy Díaz said through interpreter Kevin Vera. “This is just the beginning, and in our minds, the biggest and the most important celebration is the World Series one.”
This is the fifth division title in franchise history, joining 2008, ‘10 and ‘20-21. It’s the fourth time the Rays have claimed the AL’s best record, as they also did so in 2010, ‘20 and ‘21. And they found it fitting to clinch this time while debuting new road jerseys that put their home region front and center.
“Sitting there in the ninth inning, watching that with ‘Tampa Bay’ across our chests, with all that this franchise has been through in this past year, man, it's a great time to be a fan of the Tampa Bay Rays,” Rays CEO Ken Babby said. “So proud of this group.”
For all the questions they've faced, the Rays have spent nearly the entire season as the top team in the AL. Tuesday was their 88th consecutive day in first place, dating back to June 27, and their 128th day overall atop the AL East standings.
“To have the opportunity to run the race from start to finish is special,” Rasmussen said. “We know this isn't the finish line. We know that this is a regular-season accomplishment. 
“But man, it feels really good.”
While other contenders have risen, fallen, surged and struggled behind them, the Rays haven’t had a full month with a losing record all season. And they aren’t taking their foot off the gas, having won nine of their last 11 games while putting together an MLB-best 40-19 record since July 20.
That felt like an appropriate date to look back on Tuesday morning, when the Rays reported to Yankee Stadium knowing that just one win in this series would seal the deal. It was, as Walls put it, “a pivotal moment” in Tampa Bay’s season.
Coming out of the All-Star break, the Rays were swept by the Red Sox in a four-game series at Fenway Park from July 17-19. Maybe their nice little run was nearing an end.
But then Martinez scaled the mound and fired six strong innings in Toronto, providing leadership on and off the field, as he’s done all season. The Rays won three straight against the Blue Jays, followed that up with a winning homestand, then reeled off a perfect 9-0 road trip out west.
They haven’t looked back since.
“You can tell a lot about a team with how they respond to something like that,” Walls said. “Just being able to stop the bleeding when it's happening, being able to get back up, get going, focus on what's ahead of you and not focus too much on the past -- I feel like that's kind of been the difference this year.”
Ask around the clubhouse about where that consistency comes from, and you’ll hear different versions of the same answer. It’s chemistry that carried them through the course of the season, the bond that brought them together and the belief that they could do what nobody else expected.
“I'm very happy, very happy, because this is a special group,” Junior Caminero said. “When I got to Spring Training, first day, I [saw] this group, and I [told] them, ‘We've got to play [in] October this year.’
“And we did it.”

item.content:encoded:
When Aaron Judge is healthy, he’s the most dangerous hitter in baseball. Sometimes I get alarmed at how uncontroversial a statement that is; ours is a sport that so frequently humiliates those who make such sweeping, unequivocal judgments as those.
But the empirical evidence is what it is. Judge has played 150 or more games in a season four times in his career. In those four seasons, he’s led all position players in WAR four times and led the league in wRC+ three times. He’s been named AL MVP three times and finished second once, ahead of some real doozies: Cal Raleigh’s 60-homer year, Bobby Witt Jr.’s 10.5-WAR campaign in 2024, Shohei Ohtani’s best pitching season — in fact, a healthy Judge is the only thing that’s ever trumped a healthy Ohtani in an MVP race.
So again, it’s not uncontroversial to say that when Judge is healthy he’s the best hitter in the world. He has not, however, always been healthy. Least of all this season, when he missed three months with a broken rib. And now, the single-season AL home run king is back on the IL with a calf strain. The timing could not be worse.
Judge last played on Wednesday, leaving open the option to activate him on Sunday for the final game of the regular season. That seems like a theoretical concern at the moment rather than a practical one. Our Matt Martell was at Yankee manager Aaron Boone’s pregame media availability on Tuesday morning, where Boone illustrated the inadequacy of a return-to-play timeline at this point in the season.
“We’re planning on [Judge] not being a part of [the Wild Card Series],” Boone said. “You hear all the time with injuries, we give ranges: two to four weeks, four to six. They’re ranges for a reason. We’re at a point in the year where, obviously, we’d push it a little bit if that was in play, but that’s a week away. I’m not expecting it, but I’m not ruling it out either.”
That’s the problem. A range of two weeks in recovery time isn’t a big deal in a six-month season, but even one week is twice as long as the Yankees’ entire first playoff round. And muscle injuries can be finicky to begin with — you go to bed one night feeling fine and wake up the next morning with weakness or stiffness.
For what it’s worth, the Yankees are technically still alive in the AL East race as of this writing, but you can forgive Boone for speaking as if the division is already lost.
Either way, in order to speed things along, Judge received a platelet-poor plasma (PPP) injection on Monday, not to be confused with a platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection.
Now, apparently having read The Magic School Bus Inside the Human Body as a child is not a sufficient qualification to perform surgery on live patients. At least, that’s what the police told me. But anyone who’s read that book can tell you the makeup of human blood: Red blood cells, which carry oxygen; white blood cells, which fight infection; platelets, which stop bleeding and heal wounds; and plasma, which is the broth all the other stuff floats around in.
PRP injections are a pretty common treatment for sports injuries, but taking the healing bits out of plasma seems kind of counterintuitive. Sort of like a vodka-poor screwdriver. But evidently PPP contains high levels of fibrinogen, which is itself a healing agent. Ms. Frizzle didn’t cover fibrinogen, but sure, I’ll buy it.
Unless the PPP works an actual miracle, though, it looks like the Yankees are going to have to navigate at least the first round of the playoffs without their best player.
And even if Judge does return — either in the Wild Card round or later, if the Yankees advance — I’d caution against assuming that we’d be seeing the best of him right off the proverbial bat. For starters, 99% of star athletes in history are going to try to force their way into the lineup for the playoffs regardless of whether they’re actually healthy.
To say nothing of the fact that Judge can be streaky. This is the nature of Judge’s unusual skill set; there are 1,073 hitters in major league history with at least 5,000 career plate appearances. Judge is the only one of those who’s produced one of the three true outcomes (home run, strikeout, walk) in more than half of his career plate appearances. (I’d like to express my immense gratitude to Adam Dunn, who has a career TTO% of 49.9, for making this fun fact possible.)
Living on the extremes, as he does, Judge will have weeks where he homers every night, and others where he goes 1-for-20 with 12 strikeouts. But you live with it because, over a long enough timeline, it works out heavily in his favor. Among hitters with at least 5,000 career plate appearances, Judge has the third-highest career wRC+, trailing only Babe Ruth and Ted Williams. If you wanted to go further than “best hitter now” and anoint Judge the best hitter ever, leaning heavily on the argument that quality of competition increases over time, you’d have a credible case.
But that’s not what the Yankees got out of Judge this year. In 66 regular-season games, he’s hit .241/.360/.511, with his highest strikeout rate (29.8%) since 2019 and lowest wRC+ (141) since 2020. In seven games since he returned from his rib injury, Judge was just 4-for-23 with one home run, one walk, and 13 strikeouts.
I’ve done enough of these injury reaction posts to figure out that they’re not really about the guy who got hurt, but about the teammates he’s leaving behind.
And I don’t want to underrate the value of Judge — even the version of Judge that has a 141 wRC+, rather than a 200 wRC+ — but the Yankees have done OK without him.
In the weakest American League field in decades, the Yankees are one of only two teams with a winning percentage of .550 or better. Entering their doubleheader with the Rays on Tuesday, the Yankees are still first in the AL in home runs (216) and second in runs scored per game (4.60). Even without Judge (or Giancarlo Stanton, for that matter), their lineup has plenty of beef.

Ben Rice in particular has been absolutely terrific this season. He’s fourth among qualified AL hitters in wRC+ and third in both home runs and runs scored. The Astros have AL MVP frontrunner Yordan Alvarez in their lineup; apart from him, is there any hitter in the AL bracket who’s been Rice’s equal this year? Maybe Junior Caminero? Willson Contreras, if you value OBP over raw power? Even if you’re being charitable, it’s a short list.
Now, past Rice, things get interesting, because if you want to talk about the Yankees’ offensive depth, you have to be able to hold multiple ideas in your head at once.
As of Tuesday morning, the Yankees have 11 hitters with double-digit home runs this season, which is tied for the most in the league. That’s just counting players who have hit 10 or more home runs in pinstripes, and the Yankees brought in substantial reinforcements midseason. Luis García Jr. has just seven homers for the Yankees but 30 overall. Heliot Ramos has four home runs in 32 games and 13 overall, with 20-plus in each of his previous two seasons. George Lombard Jr. has just five home runs in 37 major league games, but he hit 12 dingers in 78 minor league games before he got called up.
Count all this up and the Yankees have more hitters with at least decent pop than they can fit on the roster at once.
At the same time, Rice is the only Yankee with 20 home runs in pinstripes this year. So while this lineup is short on automatic outs, if Judge is out, there’s a massive drop-off after Rice.
If you take Judge out of the picture, Cody Bellinger is second on the Yankees in wRC+, at 119. The Rays don’t have anyone with 100 or more plate appearances and a better wRC+ than Rice this season, but they have four hitters (Caminero, Yandy Díaz, Jonathan Aranda, and Victor Mesa Jr.) with 100 or more plate appearances and a better wRC+ than Bellinger. So do the Rangers (Justin Foscue, Josh Jung, Joc Pederson, Wyatt Langford). The Astros have Alvarez, plus Isaac Paredes and Jeremy Peña. The White Sox have Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami, and Tristan Peters.
As good as Rice has been, the Yankees’ lineup looks concerningly pedestrian without Judge. If you aren’t already a FanGraphs Member, please consider becoming one; it’s the only way to get trenchant original analysis like this.
The good news is that Judge’s calf injury runs counter to the rest of the team’s injury luck. Carlos Rodón, who missed almost three months with an elbow injury earlier this year, dominated the Rays in eight scoreless innings in Game 1 of a doubleheader on Tuesday. The same day, the Yankees activated Chisholm, who’d spent two weeks on the IL with a sprained thumb. Clarke Schmidt just returned from Tommy John surgery last week, and while he suffered biceps cramping in the bullpen on Sunday, it appears to be a minor setback. Trent Grisham remains a question mark for the start of the playoffs as he recovers from a hamstring injury, but his prognosis also looks good.
Judge is as important to the Yankees as any two or three other players put together, but with a healthy and deep rotation and Rice leading the way offensively, they’re not in bad shape. The remainder of this roster could easily survive and advance through a weaker AL bracket, setting the stage for a dramatically timed Judge return in mid-October. Like Kirk Gibson, only bigger.
Michael is a writer at FanGraphs. Previously, he was a staff writer at The Ringer and D1Baseball, and his work has appeared at Grantland, Baseball Prospectus, The Atlantic, ESPN.com, and various ill-remembered Phillies blogs. Follow him on Twitter, if you must, @MichaelBaumann.

The chances are now paper thin after a series loss in Arizona, but if the Yankees are to have any shot of chasing down the Rays in the final week of the season, they absolutely must sweep this four-game series. That required a dominant performance from Carlos Rodón facing one of the AL’s best starters in Nick Martinez. They certainly got that, Rodón running rampant for eight scoreless innings, achieving both the 1,500th strikeout and 100th win of his career as the Yankees took the first game of the day’s doubleheader, 2-0.
Rodón burst out of the gate like he had a point to prove, whiffing the first two batters of the game Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda on a pair of filthy sliders. Cam Schlittler and Max Fried are likely locks for the postseason rotation, meaning if the Yankees elect to stick with a three-man unit, that final spot comes down to Rodón and Gerrit Cole. Aaron Boone has affirmed his commitment to Cole as the Game One starter in a prospective Wild Card Series. This seemingly leaves Rodón on the bubble, which might explain the extra edge he was pitching with this afternoon.
His teammates didn’t do themselves any favors early, burning both ABS challenges in the first inning. I expect the Yankees to tighten the strings on who gets to challenge and in what situation come the playoffs as you cannot deprive yourself of such a vital tool with eight innings still to play.
Martinez entered this game with the lowest walk rate of any qualified starter and among the league’s best at limiting hard contact. He was true to form going the first turn through the order without allowing a base runner. He was helped by the collectively poor approach from the lineup, with four out of the nine batters including the side in the third striking out against a pitcher with the lowest strikeout rate among qualified starters.
That started to change the second turn through the order, the Yankees finally starting to do some damage against the high volume of pitches Martinez was throwing over the heart of the plate, starting with a Ben Rice double into the corner in right to lead off the fourth. The very next pitch Martinez threw rocketed out of the yard, Cody Bellinger blasting a first pitch sinker into the seats in right for a two-run homer — his fifth homer in the last 12 games.
George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones singled with two outs to put runners on the corners. Jones then stole second unopposed, but Anthony Volpe struck out swinging to strand the pair in scoring position. They kept up the pressure in the fifth, José Caballero reaching on a bunt single against his former team and then stealing second and third followed by a Rice walk to put runners on the corners with one out. However, Bellinger popped out and Heliot Ramos flew out as they stranded a pair in consecutive frames.
Rodón settled into an impressive groove after a Chandler Simpson single in the second, retiring the next ten batters in order until Victor Mesa Jr. led off the sixth with a single. After Rodón whiffed Jorge Mateo on a slider for his sixth strikeout, he got Richie Palacios to line out to left. Mesa was running on the play and momentarily forget he had to sprint back to first, allowing Bellinger to throw an absolute seed to Luis García Jr., who applid the tag for the inning-ending double play.
With Rodón’s pitch count standing at just 89 after seven, Boone decided to go batter-to-batter in the eighth. However, Rodón ensured his manager had no choice to make, completing the eighth inning on just seven pitches, including the 1,500th strikeout of his career. It’s tied for his longest start as a Yankee, matching the eight innings he pitched against the Cubs on July 11, 2025.
Rodón entered this start as perhaps the Yankees’ most in-form pitcher behind Schlittler. Including today, in his last eight starts, Rodón has a 1.67 ERA while holding batters to a measly .134 batting average against. He had all his pitches working today, but this really felt like a throwback to his peak years with Chicago and San Francisco. He got whiffs in bunches on the four-seamer above the zone and slider below it. In likely his penultimate start of the regular season, Rodón dominated for eight scoreless innings, allowing three hits and no walks while striking out eight to lower his ERA to 2.67 on the year.
The Yankees didn’t manage another base runner in the final three innings, but Rodón made sure that it wouldn’t come back to haunt them. David Bednar pitched a one-two-three ninth to secure his 35th save of the season. The gap to the Rays now stands at five games as the Yankees become the second team in the AL to 90 wins. At worst, they have clinched the four seed in the AL, guaranteeing home field advantage in a prospective AL Wild Card Series.
The Yankees have a few hours’ rest before taking the field again tonight. Max Fried starts the night game of the doubleheader against Drew Rasmussen. First pitch is scheduled for 7:05 pm ET with the broadcast remaining on YES, so stick around!

The New York Yankees are coming off two straight losses in Arizona to the Diamondbacks, a setback that left them a full six games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League East pennant race.
But the Yankees still have a chance to win the division and with it, the top seed in the AL and a bye out of the wild-card playoff round.
The Yankees and Rays open a four-game, head-to-head series with the first game of a doubleheader Tuesday at Yankee Stadium. With a four-game sweep, the Yankees would take the season series. They would then need to sweep the Baltimore Orioles while the Rays lose two of three to the Philadelphia Phillies, or win two of three from Baltimore while the Rays are swept, to finish tied or ahead.
Before Game 1 of the doubleheader, the Yankees announced a decision on how they will utilize veteran first baseman Paul Goldschmidt.
Goldschmidt is out of the New York Yankees lineup for a third consecutive start, out of the lineup again because of a stark platoon split against right-handed pitching.
The pattern has held all September, and it likely has fans wondering about how much longer the 39-year-old holds even a part-time role with October two weeks away.

Boone’s Platoon Explains Goldschmidt Sit
Aaron Boone’s lineup card for Tuesday’s series opener against Tampa Bay leaves Goldschmidt out again, extending a run that traces back to Saturday. He started Friday against left-hander Eduardo Rodriguez in Arizona and went 1-for-4 with a walk and two runs, then sat both weekend games against right-handers Brandon Pfaadt and Corbin Burnes. That’s three benchings in the last three games against right-handed starters.
Why? Goldschmidt has produced an elite 1.006 OPS against lefties this season but an anemic .572 mark versus right-handers, a gap wide enough that Boone starts Ben Rice at DH and Luis García Jr. at first whenever a right-hander pitches. An The Athletic report on the lineup moves after Aaron Judge’s calf strain named Goldschmidt and Heliot Ramos as the bats Boone leans on against lefties, with García handling the right-handed side.
Nick Martinez, Tuesday’s Tampa Bay starter, has largely dominated Goldschmidt in his career. The former National League MVP is 2-for-10 with four walks and two strikeouts against Martinez, and he is 0-for-13 with four strikeouts in his last three meetings with the right-hander since 2024. Martinez enters at 15-4 with a 2.94 ERA this year, and beat the Yankees in the Bronx in May, giving Boone both the season splits and the head-to-head history pointing toward a Goldschmidt benching.
Tuesday’s day-night doubleheader against two more right-handed Rays starters gives Boone an easy excuse to sit the 39-year-old.

Goldschmidt’s Future in New York
Goldschmidt becomes a free agent again this winter, and the Yankees have made no public commitment either way. A cheap return as a lefty-masher and clubhouse mentor remains plausible given Rice’s grip on first base, and his credentials, a 2022 NL MVP award, seven All-Star selections, four Gold Gloves and five Silver Sluggers still make him a name teams will inquire about this winter.
First base belongs to Rice, who has grown into an everyday role with 39 home runs and 95 RBI this season, pushing Goldschmidt into a complementary, short-side platoon job. That role fits the final stretch of a one-year, $4 million contract that can grow by $500,000 at each of four plate-appearance thresholds, according to Spotrac, a modest deal compared with the $12.5 million he earned in his first Yankees season a year earlier.

item.content:encoded:
The Colorado Rockies are 57–99.
Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player
An absurd rule for absurd times: if the worst team in baseball could steal one player from a playoff club, who should the Rockies take?
One more loss will give them their fourth consecutive 100-loss season, and they are almost certainly going to finish with the worst record in baseball.
These are absurd times for the Rockies, so I have devised an appropriately absurd rule to help them out.
The team with the worst record in baseball gets to steal one player from a playoff team.
There are, naturally, some restrictions. We’re freezing the playoff field as it stood before games on Sunday, September 20. The player has to come from one of those 12 teams, cannot be a pending free agent, and you cannot take the player who leads his team in FanGraphs WAR. The Rockies also inherit the player’s existing contract.
No, one player is not suddenly turning the Rockies into a contender. But could one poached superstar at least keep this thing from becoming five consecutive 100-loss seasons?
Here’s the board:
| Team | Off limits: fWAR leader | Highest available fWAR | Other players worth considering |
| Rays | Junior Caminero (5.2) | Drew Rasmussen (4.7) | Jonathan Aranda (3) |
| Guardians | Parker Messick (4.6) | Steven Kwan (3.4) | Gavin Williams (3.4), Brayan Rocchio (3.3), José Ramírez (2.2) |
| Rangers | Ezequiel Duran (4.6) | Jacob deGrom (4.2) | Josh Jung (2.9), Wyatt Langford (2.8) |
| Yankees | Cam Schlittler (6.1) | Ben Rice (4) | Cody Bellinger (3.9), Aaron Judge (2) |
| Red Sox | Willson Contreras (4.1) | Payton Tolle (4) | Ceddanne Rafaela (3.9), Ranger Suárez (3.7) |
| White Sox | Miguel Vargas (5) | Chase Meidroth (4) | Tristan Peters (3.9), Sean Burke (3.1) |
| Brewers | Jacob Misiorowski (6.3) | Brice Turang (5.4) | Jackson Chourio (4), Jake Bauers (3.6) |
| Dodgers | Shohei Ohtani (6.7) | Yoshinobu Yamamoto (4.7) | Max Muncy (4.3), Andy Pages (3.9) |
| Braves | Chris Sale (5.7) | Michael Harris II (4) | Matt Olson (4), Drake Baldwin (3.1) |
| Cubs | Pete Crow-Armstrong (10.2) | Alex Bregman (5) | Dansby Swanson (3.6) |
| Padres | Fernando Tatis Jr. (5) | Jackson Merrill (4) | Ty France (3.8), Mason Miller (3.7) |
| Phillies | Cristopher Sánchez (5.8) | Jesús Luzardo (5.6) | Zack Wheeler (3.5), Bryce Harper (3.4) |
For me, the choice comes down to Brice Turang, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Aaron Judge.
Turang is probably the sensible choice.
At 5.4 fWAR, he would easily lead the Rockies, giving them a legitimate top-end player while immediately solving second base for the foreseeable future. He’s 26, hitting .266/.367/.441 with an .808 OPS, and brings value on both sides of the ball with elite range, strong baserunning and a 95th-percentile walk rate.
It would be a very easy way to make the roster better.
But the Rockies really need starting pitching.
Enter Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He’s 14–8 with a 2.51 ERA, 178 strikeouts and a 0.87 WHIP over 179 innings. His Statcast profile is just as impressive: 100th-percentile pitching run value, 99th-percentile fastball run value, 95th-percentile offspeed run value and a 91st-percentile xERA.
Pitchers are risky, and Yamamoto comes with a lot of money attached. But it’s hard to argue with either the profile or the results, and the addition of the Penner family makes absorbing that contract a lot easier to imagine.
Speaking of high-priced items...
Aaron Judge.
Judge being available is basically a loophole created by our own stupid rule. Injuries have limited him to just 285 plate appearances, which is why he sits at only 2 fWAR, but he’s still hitting .241/.360/.511 with 15 home runs.
And the underlying numbers are still very much Judge: a .396 xwOBA, .569 xSLG, 94.0 mph average exit velocity and a 57.5% hard-hit rate.
It is very hard to look at that and say, “No thanks.”
After all, Aaron Judge is the type of hitter that, if he were playing 81 games a year at Coors Field, I might take out a small loan for season tickets.
So who are you stealing?

item.content:encoded:
The Yankees’ odds of winning the AL East are down to 2.8 percent per FanGraphs after getting walked off by the Diamondbacks last night. I know mathematically that makes sense, but the chances mentally feel even more extreme. I’ve been having “fun” (or whatever) comping the odds to certain pitchers from history getting a hit. We are the dregs. Remember mid-2000s Mets pitcher Aaron Heilman? I personally remember him most for giving up the homer to Yadier Molina late in Game 7 of the 2006 NLCS, just before Adam Wainwright famously caught Carlos Beltrán looking to win the pennant.
Anyway, Heilman was a horrendous hitter. He singled once in his rookie year, and then never got another hit. He ended his career 1-for-47, so an .021 average. So the Yankees just need magic only a little bit more sufficient than that RBI single by Heilman off Sidney Ponson on August 12, 2003! Hell yeah.
It’s not happening, but we press on because it’s good to check up on what everyone else is doing anyway. Here’s what was going on Saturday.
Tampa Bay Rays (94-60) 2, Boston Red Sox (84-71) 1
The Yankees gained a full game on the Rays on Friday for the first time in over a week, as Boston snapped their six-game winning streak. There was no such fortune to be found yesterday though; Tampa Bay made sure of that well before first pitch in Arizona, and it only got worse from there. By the end of the night, the Rays once again had a five-game lead over the Yanks; Tampa Bay’s magic number (combination of Rays wins or Yankees losses) to clinch the AL East is four.
This one was a pitchers’ duel to the bitter end. Brayan Bello had easily his best outing of a turbulent season (and probably the best of his career), firing eight shutout frames at the Trop and fanning 11 Rays, tying a personal best from July 9, 2024. As he only went 5.1 in that one and faced merely the soon-to-depart-Oakland A’s rather than the division-leading Rays.
The only true blemish on Bello’s record came when Jonathan Aranda cracked an opposite-field homer to make it a 1-1 game in the fourth. Tampa Bay had a chance to make it 2-1 against Bello in the seventh when Liam Hicks and Chandler Simpson led off with singles. Bello then induced a grounder from Victor Mesa Jr. to move up the runners, and then another off the bat of Richie Palacios to Trevor Story, who nailed pinch-runner Jonny DeLuca at home. Palacios swiped second, but Bello fanned Cedric Mullins to end the inning. The Rays went down in order in the eighth to end Bello’s brilliant night.
Unfortunately for Bello, a win wasn’t in the cards because Boston put up next to nothing against Freddy Peralta and the Rays’ pitching staff. Doubles by Caleb Durbin and Roman Anthony gave the Red Sox their one run in the second, but they were stymied from there. They had chances!
- Second inning after Anthony’s two-out double: Mickey Gasper lineout to center
- Fourth inning with runners on first and second, one out: Story strikeout, Durbin popout
- Fifth inning with runner on second, one out: Anthony groundout, Gasper strikeout
- Sixth inning with runners on first and second, two out: Durbin fly out to left
- Eighth inning after Adley Rutschman’s one-out double: Wilyer Abreu strikeout, Nick Sogard lineout
Even against lockdown Rays closer Bryan Baker, Boston had one last shot to take a late lead. After Story grounded out, Durbin lined a double down the left field line to put himself in scoring position for Jarren Duran. Durbin darted from second, however, and got thrown out stealing third. Duran promptly followed with a triple over DeLuca’s head in center. Isiah Kiner-Falefa bounced one to Junior Caminero at third to end the threat.
Granted a chance to walk it off, Tampa Bay didn’t waste it. Rather than blasting a homer to finish the game as he had twice earlier this homestand, Caminero began the ninth against Garrett Whitlock with a single to left. (A catwalk curtailed Durbin’s effort to catch a popup earlier in the AB.) DeLuca popped up, but Chandler Simpson grounded one through the six-hole for another hit. The runners moved up when catcher Connor Wong let a Whitlock sinker up bounce off his glove for a passed ball. Palacios ended the night with flare to center that fell in, securing the win for Tampa Bay. At least the Wild Card Series is also almost certainly going to be at Yankee Stadium now, I suppose.
AL Rock Fight
Cleveland Guardians (80-75) 12, The Athletics (61-94) 6
Two crooked numbers effectively decided Saturday’s affair with the A’s in a hurry. Tanner Bibee kind of stunk and would allow six runs in a dozen hits while failing to make through five, but it hardly mattered. Cleveland erased a 2-0 deficit in the first on a three-run shot from rookie Chase DeLauter and two-run homer by Angel Martinez. The A’s got one back in the third, only to see another five-spot from the Guardians on poor Jacob Lopez as David Fry, Austin Hedges, and Brayan Rocchio all delivered RBI doubles. Martinez later added a homer and an RBI single in a career-best four-hit day.
Chicago White Sox (79-76) 3, Detroit Tigers (73-82) 1
Cleveland’s win meant that Chicago was stuck at a game back in the AL Central in the best-case, but they did at least help push one of their Wild Card foes out of the picture with a win. Honestly, this was probably kind of a dud of a game for anyone who isn’t a White Sox fan, the lone highlights being Sean Burke’s six scoreless frames and Miguel Vargas’ sixth-inning solo shot to make it 3-1, Chicago (the other runs scored on an RBI single by Munetaka Murakami and a fifth-inning sac fly). Spencer Torkelson had a chance to tie the game with a homer following Hao-Yu Lee’s two-out single in the ninth, but he flew out to center to end it.
Milwaukee Brewers (97-58) 1, Baltimore Orioles (75-80) 0
Yeah, it’s time to stick a fork in the O’s. It was all but certain for awhile now, but Chicago’s win combined with Baltimore’s second-straight loss to Milwaukee means that the Orioles are four back with a week to play, plus multiple teams in front of them. Trevor Rogers was the hard-luck loser here while Baltimore got blanked on four hits and Rece Hinds lost a fly ball from Joey Ortiz in the sun, allowing him to triple and score on Gary Sánchez’s RBI grounder. Woof.
Texas Rangers (78-77) 6, Toronto Blue Jays (76-79) 1
The O’s aren’t the only bird that are all but shot down, either. Trade Deadline acquisition José Soriano coughed up an early homer to Josh Jung, beginning a five-inning, six-run outing that pushed Toronto three games out in the Wild Card and the Rangers into a one-game AL West lead over Houston. The only downside for Texas was that second-half surprise Cal Quantrill—who has a 1.75 ERA since re-entering the rotation in late July—left in the second with lat tightness, so old friend Jordan Montgomery picked up the slack in long relief, retiring 11 of the 12 hitters he faced with no hits allowed.
Atlanta Braves (91-64) 6, Houston Astros (77-78) 3
Houston and Texas have been wrestling all week over the prestigious “Who can win this horri-awful division with a .500-ish record” crown. Sunday it went to Texas with the Astros falling out of their tie for first place (remember that they own the tiebreaker). Isaac Paredes had put Houston ahead with a solo homer and an RBI knock in the third, but the Astros’ bullpen set that lead on fire. The big blow came off the bat of Ronald Acuña Jr., who belted a grand slam off Bryan Abreu in the seventh after AJ Blubaugh made a right mess of things.

The Boston Red Sox and Tampa Bay Rays head into Sunday’s series finale at Fenway Park with the three-game set knotted at one win apiece after Saturday’s 2-1 Rays victory.
Left-hander Patrick Sandoval takes the mound for Boston against Tampa Bay right-hander Griffin Jax, a matchup that carries extra weight with the regular season winding down and playoff positioning still in flux.
Interim manager Chad Tracy has kept the bulk of his starting nine intact, but he has made a modest yet noticeable adjustment involving outfielder Jarren Duran, via Underdog MLB.
After sitting out the series opener and batting eighth on Saturday, Duran will slide up one spot into the seventh hole. He will hit in front of Isaiah Kiner-Falefa and Nate Eaton while remaining in center field, the position he has occupied since injuries to Ceddanne Rafaela and Eli White opened the job.
The rest of the order features Roman Anthony in left, Mickey Gasper at designated hitter, Adley Rutschman behind the plate, Trevor Story at shortstop, Nick Sogard at first, and Cooper Durbin at third.
The move comes during a difficult individual season for Duran. Entering Sunday he is hitting .206 in 144 games, with 65 runs, 110 hits, 20 home runs and 69 RBIs. His slugging percentage sits at .364 and his OPS at .626.
Speculation about a possible trade lingered for weeks before the August 4 deadline, yet Duran remained in a Red Sox uniform and has continued to receive regular playing time as the club pushes toward October.
Boston sits at 84-71 with seven games left and occupies what currently looks like the second American League Wild Card spot. Should the standings hold, the Red Sox would open the postseason on the road in a best-of-three Wild Card series against the New York Yankees.
Every remaining game, including Sunday’s finale against a familiar division rival, therefore carries playoff implications.
Tracy’s decision to bump Duran up in the order is a small tactical shift rather than a wholesale overhaul, but it signals a willingness to tinker as the club tries to generate more consistent offense down the stretch.
Whether the extra spot in the lineup produces results remains to be seen.
Duran’s season-long struggles have been well documented, yet he has shown flashes of the power and speed that once made him a fixture in the middle of Boston’s order.
A productive afternoon against Jax and the Rays would give the Red Sox a series victory and a bit of momentum heading into the final week.
With the calendar now late September and the postseason picture still taking shape, even incremental lineup changes can feel significant.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Richie Palacios dropped a blooper into shallow right in the ninth inning to score Junior Caminero and give the Tampa Bay Rays a 2-1 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Saturday.
Tampa Bay, which has three walk-off wins on its current homestand, lowered its magic number to clinch the AL East to five games. The second-place Yankees are in Arizona on Saturday night.
Prior to Palacios’ single, the Rays were 0 for 17 with runners in scoring position over the first two games of the series. The postseason-bound Rays, who’ve won seven of their last eight, capitalized on two fortuitous bounces in the ninth.
First, Caminero’s foul popup bounced off the Tropicana Field catwalk and out of the reach of third baseman Caleb Durbin. Caminero then lined the next pitch from Garrett Whitlock (7-2) into left. Three batters later, after Chandler Simpson singled, Connor Wong’s passed ball moved Caminero to third.
Bidding to clinch a wild-card berth, the Red Sox squandered a prime opportunity in the top of the ninth.
Facing closer Bryan Baker (4-2) in a tie game, Boston got a double from Caleb Durbin and a triple from Jarren Duran. However, Nick Fortes threw out Durbin stealing third before Duran’s triple, and Caminero made a stellar play at third base to retire Isiah Kiner-Falefa, stranding Duran.
Boston also wasted a phenomenal effort from starter Brayan Bello, who matched a career high with 11 strikeouts. In eight innings, he allowed five hits, one run and no walks. Red Sox closer Aroldis Chapman (lat tightness) was unavailable.
The Red Sox took a 1-0 lead with doubles from Durbin and Roman Anthony in the third inning. Trevor Story extended his hitting streak to 10 games with a sixth-inning single.
Jonathan Aranda tied it with an opposite-field solo homer on the first pitch of the Rays’ fourth.
The Rays are an MLB-best 25-14 in one-run games.
Boston could have clinched a playoff berth with a win combined with a loss by either the Rangers or Astros. Both of those teams were seven games behind the Red Sox with eight games remaining entering Saturday.
UP NEXT
Right-hander Griffin Jax (7-10, 3.80 ERA) gets the nod for the Rays on Sunday in the series finale. Boston had not announced a starter.
